title: Integrity norms can weaken without continued enforcement even in a low-corruption setting
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35756, universe-level Singapore housing transactions linked to public-official status, planned MRT stations, enforcement changes, and survey measures
geography: Singapore public officials, their relatives, housing transactions, MRT planning, and anti-corruption enforcement

observations.period: Planned MRT station expansions, public announcements, enforcement tightening, and linked survey periods

denominator.unit: Universe-level housing transactions and public-official records; exact public abstract denominator not disclosed

informed_home_purchase.value: civil servants disproportionately bought homes near planned but not yet publicly announced MRT stations, with the effect concentrated one to two years before announcements

official_and_relative_pattern.value: the behavior was concentrated among mid-level officials and rail-planning-connected agencies and also appeared among relatives

enforcement_response.value: stronger formal enforcement substantially reduced direct and indirect misconduct

norms_and_trust.value: survey measures show changes in perceived corruption, public trust, and pro-integrity norms consistent with norms that persist but are fragile

public_legitimacy.value: not observed as a direct common outcome
public_legitimacy.unit: missing citizen-level legitimacy, reporting, service quality, and political-action outcome linked to each transaction

observations.method: Universe-level housing transaction analysis identifying informed purchases around planned but unpublished MRT stations, matched comparisons, enforcement changes, survey measures, and a dynamic model of norm persistence and policy learning.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not disclose transaction counts, exact enforcement dates, all controls, or the full survey design. The transaction pattern is evidence of information-linked misconduct in the studied setting, not a direct measure of every official's beliefs or all corruption.
observations.subgroup: Singapore civil servants, mid-level officials, rail-planning-connected agencies, and relatives; nonofficial transactions and broader public behavior are used as comparison contexts but are not fully described in the abstract.
observations.counterinterpretation: Unusual home purchases could reflect other information or housing-market differences, though the preannouncement timing and agency concentration support an information-leakage interpretation. Stronger enforcement may reduce observed misconduct through deterrence, detection, or changed reporting rather than by rebuilding norms alone.

boundary: This comparative record measures information-linked housing transactions, enforcement response, and survey/model evidence about integrity norms in Singapore. It does not establish a contemporary U.S. effect, a universal relationship between norms and corruption, or direct citizen legitimacy and political outcomes.
